units.title: The Respiratory System
units.intro:
Nose (warm, filter, moisten) → pharynx → trachea (rings of cartilage) → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli (huge surface, thin, moist, capillary wrap).

**Inhale:** diaphragm down, ribs up and out → chest volume up → pressure down → air in. **Exhale:** opposite (often passive at rest).

cards.title: 5.1.1 The Nose
body: The human respiratory system starts with the nose.
The nose encloses the nasal cavity, which opens to the outside through openings called the nostrils.
The air that enters the body through the nose is warmed, filtered and moistened as it passes through the nasal cavity.
Fine hairs (cilia) lining the cavity filter the inhaled air before it passes down the pharynx.

cards.title: 5.1.2 The Pharynx
body: **The pharynx** is a tube-like structure, and is a part of both the respiratory and digestive systems.
Air is breathed in through the trachea into the lungs, whereas food passes down the oesophagus to the stomach.
The pharynx extends into a slit or narrow opening, known as glottis, which leads into the larynx.
The opening is guarded by a flap of tissue called the epiglottis.

cards.title: 5.1.3 The Trachea
body: The trachea extends from the neck to the thorax, where it divides into the right and left main bronchi (singular: bronchus).
The two main bronchi enter the right and left lungs.
Inside the lung, each bronchus branches into several bronchioles.
A single layer of epithelial cells lines each alveolus.

cards.title: 5.1.4 The Lungs
body: The branching network of bronchi, bronchioles and alveoli comprise the lungs.
Lungs are respiratory organs found in the thoracic cavity.
The left lung is slightly smaller (because of the heart that is located slightly to the left of the body) and has two lobes.
The right lung is bigger, with three lobes.

steps.text: **Step 1: Define external respiration**
External respiration (breathing) is the exchange of respiratory gases (oxygen and carbon dioxide) between the lungs (alveoli) and the atmosphere or blood.
**Step 2: Contrast with internal respiration**
Internal or cellular respiration is the process where glucose is oxidized inside cells to yield ATP.
**Final Result:**

cards.why:
**Step 1: Recall the mechanical steps of inhalation**
During inhalation, the following occur:
* The diaphragm contracts and flattens (moves downward).
* The external intercostal muscles contract, pulling the ribs upward and outward.
* This increases the thoracic volume and decreases intra-pulmonary pressure.

**Final Result:**
**The external intercostal muscles contract, pulling the ribs upward and outward.**

**Step 2:** Identify locations. They line the nasal cavity (nose), trachea, and bronchi.

cards.title: 5.2.3 Transfer of Gases
body: In both cases, the exchange of gases is carried out by simple diffusion.
Alveoli have specific adaptations in order to carry efficient gaseous exchange.
The surface of the alveoli is kept moistened, for the gases to be dissolved and diffused easily. b.
The alveoli and capillaries have very thin walls.

cards.title: Step by step: Mechanisms of breathing
body: **Step 1:** Inhalation: the diaphragm contracts and flattens; the external intercostal muscles contract, moving the ribs up and out.
**Step 2:** This increases the volume of the chest cavity, so pressure in the lungs falls below atmospheric pressure, and air rushes in.
**Step 3:** Exhalation: the diaphragm relaxes and becomes dome-shaped; the intercostal muscles relax and the ribs move down and in.
**Step 4:** Chest volume decreases, lung pressure rises above atmospheric pressure, and air is pushed out.
**Step 5:** In the alveoli, O₂ diffuses into the blood and CO₂ diffuses out; alveoli are adapted by a huge surface area, thin walls (one cell), moisture and a rich blood supply.
**Example:** Bell-jar model: pulling the rubber sheet (diaphragm) down increases the volume inside the jar, the pressure drops and the balloons (lungs) inflate – exactly like inhalation.

cards.title: Mnemonic — "Volume Up, Pressure Down, Air In"
body: V-U, P-D, A-I (reverse everything for exhalation).

cards.title: Exam tip
body: Always link the three steps: muscle action → volume change → pressure change → air movement. Missing the pressure step is the commonest error.

cards.title: Exam question, solved
cards.problem: The tiny air sac in the lungs where gas exchange occurs is called the  A) bronchi.  B) alveoli.  C) trachea.  D) diaphragm.  E) pleura cavity.

steps.text: **Step 1.** The **alveoli** (singular: alveolus) are the tiny, balloon-like air sacs at the end of the respiratory tree.
**Step 2.** This is the exact site where oxygen enters the blood and carbon dioxide leaves the blood through thin walls.

cards.why: The **diaphragm** is a large, dome-shaped muscle located at the base of the lungs. Its contraction and relaxation change the volume and pressure of the chest cavity, which is the primary mechanism for inhalation and exhalation (breathing).

cards.title: 5.3 Cellular Respiration
body: **Cellular respiration** is a complex process of energy release from food in a cell.
Energy is released when simple sugar molecules are oxidized during a series of steps controlled by enzymes.
Respiration is initiated in the cytoplasm and completed in the mitochondria.
Respiration can be divided into two types, depending on the presence or absence of oxygen during the reaction.
**Glycolysis literally** means the “splitting of sugars”.

cards.title: Cellular Respiration
body: Gases move by diffusion: O₂ alveolus → blood; CO₂ blood → alveolus. In tissues the arrows reverse. Cellular respiration in mitochondria: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + ATP. Exercise raises rate and depth because muscles demand more ATP and make more CO₂.

cards.title: More detail — air and ATP
body: Trachea rings are C-shaped so the oesophagus can bulge when you swallow. Alveoli: millions, moist, one-cell wall, wrapped in capillaries — four features every 4-mark wants. Smoking damages cilia and alveoli (emphysema = less surface).

Aerobic respiration needs oxygen and yields much ATP. Anaerobic in muscle: glucose → lactic acid + little ATP; oxygen debt afterwards. Plants / yeast anaerobic path is different (ethanol) — don’t mix unless asked. Exercise: more CO₂ in blood → brain raises breathing rate and heart rate together.

cards.why:
**Step 1:** Identify the type of fermentation in yeast. Yeast performs **alcoholic fermentation**.
**Step 2:** Identify the products. The breakdown of glucose in the absence of oxygen yields **ethanol (alcohol)**, **carbon dioxide ($$ CO_2 $$)**, and a net gain of **2 ATP** molecules.
**Step 3:** Compare with options. Option B matches these products.

cards.title: 5.4 Effects of Physical Exercise
body: An example is the strengthening of the muscles, including the cardiovascular muscles of the heart.
Like all muscles, the heart becomes stronger and larger with regular exercise.
The heart rate of people that exercise regularly is slower because less effort is needed to pump blood.
Physical exercise involving weight lifting can improve bone density and strength.
Frequent and regular physical exercise boosts the immune system, and helps prevent illnesses such as cardiovascular diseases, diabetes and obesity.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: During strenuous exercise, the breathing rate increases mainly to ____.

options.B: supply more oxygen and remove the extra carbon dioxide produced by the muscles

cards.why:
**Step 1:** Working muscles respire faster, using more oxygen and producing more CO₂.

**Step 2:** A rise in blood CO₂ is detected by the brain, which speeds up breathing.

**Step 3:** Faster, deeper breathing brings in O₂ and removes CO₂.

**Tip:** Read every option against the rule before choosing.

questions.q: A biology class in Asmara is studying why oxygen and carbon dioxide are exchanged so rapidly inside the lungs. Which of the following combinations correctly states two structural adaptations of the alveoli that make this rapid diffusion possible?

options.A: A thick, multi-layered alveolar wall and a dry inner lining
options.B: A thin single-layer epithelial wall and a moist inner surface
options.C: Hard C-shaped cartilage rings around each alveolus and a moist inner surface
options.D: A dense network of capillaries and a thick, muscular alveolar wall

why: **Recall where exchange happens.** The unit states that the exchange of $$O_2$$ and $$CO_2$$ occurs entirely within the alveoli, and that it takes place by simple diffusion.

**Check each stated adaptation.** The unit lists three adaptations of alveoli: extremely thin walls (a single layer of flat epithelial cells, giving a very short diffusion path), a moist inner surface (so gases dissolve in water first), and a massive surface area from about 600 to 700 million alveoli.

**Test the options.** Option A is wrong because the alveolar wall is one cell thick, not thick and multi-layered, and the surface is moist, not dry. Option C is wrong because cartilage rings belong to the trachea, not to alveoli. Option D is wrong because a thick muscular wall would lengthen the diffusion path.
**Conclude.** Option B alone names two genuine adaptations: the thin single-layer epithelial wall and the moist inner surface.
questions.tip: Eliminate options that contradict the unit notes, then choose the one that matches every detail in the question.

questions.q: During a hospital visit in Keren, a student is told that a patient's lungs contain roughly 600 to 700 million tiny air sacs. Which of the following best explains why this huge number of alveoli is important for the patient?
questions.answer: C. It creates a massive surface area for gas exchange by diffusion.
why: **Recall the third adaptation.** The unit states that the lungs contain approximately 600 to 700 million alveoli surrounded by a dense capillary network, providing a massive surface area for gas exchange.
**Link structure to function.** Simple diffusion is faster when more surface is available, so a large total alveolar surface increases the rate of $$O_2$$ uptake and $$CO_2$$ removal.

**Check the distractors.** Option A is wrong because surface area does not warm the air; warming and filtering happen in the nasal cavity. Option B is wrong because the total distance for diffusion is set by the thinness of the walls, not by the number of alveoli. Option D is wrong because the volume of each individual alveolus is microscopic, not large.
**Conclude.** The large number of alveoli matters because it maximises the surface area available for diffusion.

why: **Recall the first adaptation.** The unit states that the walls of both the alveoli and the surrounding capillaries consist of a single layer of flat epithelial cells, creating an incredibly short diffusion path.
**Relate thickness to diffusion.** The shorter the distance a gas must travel, the faster it diffuses across the membranes, so a one-cell-thick barrier speeds up $$O_2$$ and $$CO_2$$ movement.

**Eliminate the distractors.** Option B is wrong because thin walls do not generate the pressure that drives ventilation; the diaphragm and intercostal muscles do. Option C is wrong because mucus and cilia for trapping dust are found in the nasal cavity and airways. Option D is wrong because the air inside the alveoli is warm because the nose warmed it before it arrived, not because the wall is thin.
**Conclude.** The single-cell thickness exists to minimise the diffusion distance.

questions.q: In a school laboratory in Asmara, a group of Grade 10 students estimated that a small section of lung tissue they examined provided a total surface area for gaseous exchange of $$5.0 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m}^2$$. The average surface area of a single alveolus is $$1.0 \times 10^{-7}\ \text{m}^2$$. Calculate the number of alveoli present in that small section of lung tissue.
why: **Identify the given values.** Total surface area of the section $$= 5.0 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m}^2$$. Average surface area of one alveolus $$= 1.0 \times 10^{-7}\ \text{m}^2$$.

**State the working formula.** Since the total surface area is supplied by many identical alveoli, the number of alveoli is found by dividing the total surface area by the surface area of one alveolus: $$\text{Number of alveoli} = \dfrac{\text{Total surface area}}{\text{Surface area of one alveolus}}$$.
**Substitute the values.** $$\text{Number of alveoli} = \dfrac{5.0 \times 10^{-3}}{1.0 \times 10^{-7}}$$.

**Carry out the arithmetic.** Dividing the coefficients gives $$5.0 \div 1.0 = 5.0$$, and dividing the powers of ten gives $$10^{-3} \div 10^{-7} = 10^{-3-(-7)} = 10^{4}$$. Therefore the number of alveoli $$= 5.0 \times 10^{4}$$.
**Conclude.** The small section of lung tissue contains $$5.0 \times 10^{4}$$ alveoli, that is 50,000 alveoli, which shows how densely packed the gas-exchange surface is.

questions.q:
Complete the following statements about the mechanism of breathing.
(a) During inhalation the diaphragm ________ and moves downward, while the external intercostal muscles contract and pull the ribs ________ and outward.
(b) As a result the volume of the thoracic cavity ________, and the pressure inside the alveoli becomes ________ than atmospheric pressure, so air flows into the lungs.
(c) During exhalation at rest, the diaphragm relaxes and arches upward into a ________ shape.
why: **Recall the action of the muscles.** The unit states that during inhalation the diaphragm contracts and moves downward, while the external intercostal muscles contract, pulling the ribs upward and outward.

**Recall the effect on volume and pressure.** This muscular action increases the volume of the thoracic cavity, which drops the pressure inside the alveoli below atmospheric pressure, so air flows down the pressure gradient into the lungs.

**Recall exhalation at rest.** The diaphragm and intercostal muscles relax, the diaphragm moves upward into a dome shape, the ribs lower, thoracic volume decreases and alveolar pressure rises above atmospheric pressure.
**Fill the blanks.** (a) contracts; upward. (b) increases; lower. (c) dome.

questions.q: A student in Asmara is revising quietly at her desk, while her brother is sprinting in a school athletics race. Explain which form of cellular respiration each of them mainly uses in their muscle cells, and compare the amount of ATP each pathway can release from one molecule of glucose.
questions.answer: The resting student's muscle cells mainly use aerobic respiration, which releases up to $$36\text{ to } 38\ \text{ATP}$$ per glucose molecule with oxygen, while the sprinting brother's muscle cells switch to anaerobic respiration (lactic acid fermentation), which releases only $$2\ \text{ATP}$$ per glucose molecule without oxygen, making aerobic respiration about 18 to 19 times more efficient.
why: **Define cellular respiration.** Cellular respiration is the enzymatic oxidation of glucose inside cells to produce ATP. Both aerobic and anaerobic pathways begin with glycolysis, the splitting of a glucose molecule into two pyruvic acid molecules with a net gain of 2 ATP.

**Identify the pathway used at rest.** While the student is resting quietly, oxygen is plentiful, so her muscle cells use aerobic respiration. Pyruvic acid enters the mitochondria and is completely broken down in the presence of oxygen, releasing carbon dioxide, water and up to 36 to 38 ATP per glucose molecule.

**Identify the pathway used during sprinting.** During intense exercise the oxygen supplied by the lungs and blood is insufficient to meet the high ATP demand. Her brother's muscle cells therefore switch to anaerobic respiration in the cytoplasm, converting pyruvic acid into lactic acid and releasing only 2 ATP per glucose molecule.

**Compare the ATP yields.** Aerobic respiration yields about 36 to 38 ATP per glucose molecule, whereas anaerobic lactic acid fermentation yields only 2 ATP per glucose molecule, so aerobic respiration is roughly 18 to 19 times more efficient.

**Relate to the observations.** This explains why the sprinter's muscles tire quickly: lactic acid accumulation makes muscles stiff and sore, while the resting student's cells obtain far more ATP from the same amount of glucose using oxygen.

questions.q: A baker in Keren uses yeast to make bread dough rise, while a weightlifter in the same town performs a very heavy lift. State the type of respiration each process depends on and name the products formed from glucose in each case.
questions.answer: The yeast carries out anaerobic respiration (alcohol fermentation), producing ethyl alcohol and carbon dioxide with 2 ATP per glucose; the weightlifter's muscle cells carry out anaerobic respiration (lactic acid fermentation), producing lactic acid with 2 ATP per glucose.
why: **Recall the two anaerobic pathways.** The unit describes alcohol fermentation in plants, yeast and some bacteria, and lactic acid fermentation in animal muscle cells during intense exercise.

**Identify the yeast process.** In bread making, yeast converts glucose into ethyl alcohol and carbon dioxide, and this carbon dioxide is what makes the dough rise. The energy released is only 2 ATP per glucose molecule.

**Identify the weightlifter's process.** During a very heavy lift the oxygen supply to the muscles is insufficient, so pyruvic acid is converted into lactic acid, releasing 2 ATP per glucose molecule.
**Conclude with products.** Yeast: ethyl alcohol, carbon dioxide and 2 ATP. Muscle: lactic acid and 2 ATP. Both occur in the absence of oxygen.

questions.q: Explain why the lungs alone cannot move air in and out, and state which structures provide the force for breathing.
questions.answer: Lungs are soft, elastic and non-muscular, so they cannot pump air by themselves; breathing is driven by pressure differences created by the contraction and relaxation of the diaphragm and the external intercostal muscles.
why: **Describe the lung tissue.** The unit states that lungs are soft, elastic and non-muscular, so they contain no skeletal muscle of their own and cannot actively expand or contract.
**Explain the driving force.** Breathing is driven by pressure differences created by two sets of muscles: the diaphragm and the external intercostal muscles.

**Link muscle action to air flow.** On inhalation the diaphragm contracts and flattens while the intercostal muscles pull the ribs up and out, increasing thoracic volume and lowering alveolar pressure below atmospheric pressure so air flows in; on exhalation these muscles relax, thoracic volume decreases and air is pushed out.
**Conclude.** The lungs are passive; the diaphragm and intercostal muscles change the volume of the thoracic cavity and create the pressure gradients that ventilate the lungs.
